cells.verb: tending what's growing with steady, responsible care, keeping two real demands alive at once
cells.place: at the doorway where something new is coming in
cells.ask: Let one person see what you've been keeping alive and what it cost you — and let one thing that's finished be finished. What comes back is care that doesn't wear you out.
cells.core:
Something new is arriving and you're meeting it the way a good gardener meets weather: not controlling it, tending it. You've got more than one thing that needs your care right now and you're not dropping either one — you're keeping both fed, deciding where the water goes, and it's working.

What this is free to feed next: let it be seen. Show someone what you've been keeping alive and what you gave up to do it. And where something has run its course, let it go as a thing completed rather than a thing lost. That's how the tending stays light instead of becoming a load.
cells.sheetLine: You're meeting what's arriving with care, not control — and it's holding.

cells.tense: Future — bracing at a future that can't be written in.
cells.verb: tending so hard it's turned into gripping, managing what's coming before it has landed
cells.place: at the doorway where something new is coming in
cells.ask: Pick one thing that already turned out well and sit with it for an evening, letting yourself be satisfied without planning the next move. What comes back is holding what's arriving without clutching it.
cells.core:
Something's coming in and you've already got it rationed, scheduled, and protected against a future that hasn't shown up. The care is real; it's just running ahead of the thing it's caring for. Every resource gets counted twice. Every new arrival gets managed before it's had a chance to be met.

The way back isn't to loosen the grip by force. It's to feel full. Something you hoped for has actually come to pass — go stand in that for a while. Let yourself be satisfied with it, completely, without turning it into the next plan. A hand that knows it's already been given enough can open.
cells.sheetLine: You're managing what's arriving before it's had a chance to arrive.

cells.tense: Past — still standing at a door that's already behind you.
cells.verb: letting what's growing go untended, the care having gone quiet
cells.place: at the doorway where something new is coming in
cells.ask: Name one thing you still want to see grow, after everything, and go back to it tomorrow anyway. What comes back is growth that happens without forcing.
cells.core:
Something new is at the door and nobody's answering. You know how to tend things — that hasn't gone anywhere — but the tending has stopped, and what's arriving now is landing in a room where the care already left. You're facing a door that's closed, and the one that's open is behind you.

Don't try to force the care back on. Feed the thing underneath it instead: the wanting. There's something you still hope will grow, even now, even after how it's gone. Say what it is, and then show up to it once more tomorrow. The hoping is what pulls the tending back through.
cells.sheetLine: Something's arriving and the care that would meet it has gone quiet.

cells.tense: Disowned present — pen down in a room you're already writing.
cells.verb: already tending what's coming in, deciding what gets fed, and calling it just getting by
cells.place: at the doorway where something new is coming in
cells.ask: Say out loud what you've been giving up to keep this going, to one person, once. What comes back is care that stops exhausting you because it finally has a name.
cells.core:
You're already doing it. What's arriving is being met — you're choosing where the attention goes, which demand gets fed first, what gets held back for later — and you describe all of this as things just happening to you. 'I'm only dealing with what comes.' But someone is deciding, and it's you.

The cost of not claiming it is that the sacrifice goes unseen, including by you. So go back to the simplest version: what are you actually giving up to keep these things alive? Say it plainly, to one person. Once it's visible, the tending stops running on fumes.
cells.sheetLine: You're already the one tending this. You just haven't said so.

flags.detail: "a while ago" — a cell knows no one's past
